title: How does Java I/O (`DataInputStream` wrapping `BufferedInputStream` wrapping `GZIPInputStream`...) exemplify the Decorator pattern, and how does it avoid subclass explosion?
shortTitle: How Java I/O streams exemplify the Decorator pattern and avoid subclass explosion
keyPoints: Each Java stream decorator wraps another stream of the same type and adds one feature, so capabilities are stacked at runtime.
The is-a and has-a dual relationship lets a decorator be used anywhere the component is expected, including as the inner of another decorator.
`FilterInputStream` is the abstract decorator that holds a `protected volatile InputStream in` reference.
Three decorator classes give all combinations instead of eight-plus subclasses, avoiding subclass explosion.
Wrapping order matters: buffering a compressed stream differs from compressing a buffered stream.
Closing the outermost stream tears down the entire chain because each decorator's `close()` delegates inward.

s1_definition.oneliner: Each Java stream decorator wraps another stream of the same type and adds one feature, so you stack capabilities at runtime instead of building a subclass for every combination.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Decorator pattern** – attaches additional responsibilities to an object dynamically by wrapping it in another object that shares the same interface.
- **Component** – the common type, `InputStream`, that both real sources and decorators implement.
- **Concrete component** – a real source like `FileInputStream` or `ByteArrayInputStream`.
- **Abstract decorator** – `FilterInputStream`, which extends `InputStream` and holds a reference to a wrapped `InputStream`.
- **Concrete decorators** – `BufferedInputStream`, `DataInputStream`, `GZIPInputStream`, each adding exactly one capability.
- **Subclass explosion** – without decorators, every combination of features requires a separate subclass, growing combinatorially.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India sends a daily statement file. The raw file is plain data. Now you want it buffered for speed, compressed to save space, and read as structured numbers. Instead of inventing a special buffered-compressed-structured machine, you take the plain file and wrap it: first through a buffering layer, then through a decompression layer, then through a structured-reading layer. Each layer is a clip-on attachment that adds one capability and passes the data along. That snap-on-layers idea is the Decorator pattern.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Reading through a Decorator chain
  ─────────────────────────────────
  DataInputStream   ←── reads typed values (readInt, readUTF)
       │
       ▼
  BufferedInputStream ←── buffers for performance
       │
       ▼
  GZIPInputStream    ←── decompresses
       │
       ▼
  FileInputStream    ←── reads raw bytes from disk
       │
       ▼
    [ file.gz ]
```

```text
  Subclass explosion without Decorator
  ────────────────────────────────────
  3 features → 2^3 = 8 subclasses

  With Decorator:
  3 decorator classes → all 8 combinations at runtime

  FileInputStream ──→ GZIPInputStream ──→ BufferedInputStream
        │                                        │
        └────── any subset, any order ───────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The Decorator pattern attaches extra responsibilities to an object dynamically by wrapping it in another object that shares the same interface, and Java's I/O stream library is the textbook example. On the input side the common type is `InputStream`. `FileInputStream` is the concrete source that reads raw bytes, and decorators like `GZIPInputStream`, `BufferedInputStream`, and `DataInputStream` each wrap another stream, add exactly one capability, and still expose the `InputStream` interface.

The structural trick is that each decorator is-an `InputStream` and also has-an `InputStream`. Because it extends `InputStream` it can be used anywhere a stream is expected, including as the thing another decorator wraps. Because it holds an inner stream it delegates the real work and adds its own behaviour. That dual relationship lets you compose a `DataInputStream` wrapping a `BufferedInputStream` wrapping a `GZIPInputStream` wrapping a `FileInputStream`, and reading from the outer stream pulls bytes through the whole chain transparently.

The reason this matters is subclass explosion. Without decorators, combining features with inheritance would require a separate subclass for every combination and ordering, which grows as 2^n. The Decorator pattern collapses that: one class per feature, composed at runtime in whatever order you need. Three decorator classes give every combination, and adding a fourth feature is one more class rather than doubling the hierarchy.

In the banking project at National Bank of India, Rajesh uses exactly this approach to read and write compressed, buffered, structured balance-snapshot files. The two nuances to mention are that wrapping order matters, since buffering a compressed stream differs from compressing a buffered one, and that closing the outermost stream tears down the whole chain because each decorator's `close()` delegates inward.

Remember one sentence: each Java I/O decorator wraps another stream, adds one feature, and avoids subclass explosion by composing capabilities at runtime.
